title: Decolonising Museums and Restitution
welcome_lead: The Benin Bronzes, the Parthenon Marbles, and the politics of return.
meta_desc: A-Level Art & Design: decolonising museums, restitution, and contested collections.
final_note: Whose history? Whose objects? Whose museum?

concepts.def: Critically re-examining museum collections shaped by empire.
Returning objects to their place or community of origin.
Brass plaques and sculptures looted from Benin City by British forces in 1897.
Marble sculptures removed from Athens by Lord Elgin (1801-1812).
The documented history of ownership of an artwork.
2018 French report recommending wide restitution of African heritage.

walkthroughs.body_html: Many European museum collections originate in imperial expansion. The Benin Bronzes were looted from Benin City by a British 'punitive expedition' in 1897. Calls for return date back over a century.
The 2018 Sarr-Savoy Report, commissioned by President Macron, recommended that France return African heritage held in its museums. Germany has since begun returning Benin Bronzes to Nigeria.
The Parthenon Marbles, removed by Lord Elgin between 1801 and 1812, remain in the British Museum despite long-standing Greek requests for return — a paradigm case in restitution debates.
